literary_identity: Poet; colonial administrator in Ireland; the self-fashioned 'new poet' of the English Renaissance and its greatest non-dramatic poet.
biography: Born in London c. 1552, the son of a journeyman clothmaker; educated at Merchant Taylors' School under Richard Mulcaster and at Pembroke Hall, Cambridge (BA 1573, MA 1576), where he associated with Gabriel Harvey. He entered the household of the Earl of Leicester, met Sidney and Dyer in the 'Areopagus' circle, and published The Shepheardes Calender (1579) to immediate fame. In 1580 he went to Ireland as secretary to Lord Grey de Wilton and spent most of his remaining life there as a planter and official (Kilcolman Castle, Co. Cork), publishing The Faerie Queene (1590, 1596), Complaints (1591), Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), Amoretti and Epithalamion (1595), and Prothalamion (1596). In 1598 Kilcolman was burned in Tyrone's rebellion; Spenser fled to London and died there on 13 January 1599, and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Chaucer.
literary_profile: The laureate of Elizabethan England, whose career was a deliberate imitation of Virgil's — from pastoral to epic — in the service of Protestant nationhood; he made the English language the vehicle of a full-scale national epic and a new poetic idiom (the Spenserian stanza).
stylistic_characteristics: Archaizing diction ('the antique rolles'), the nine-line Spenserian stanza, elaborate allegory, musical fluency, and the fusion of Italian romance (Ariosto, Tasso), classical epic, and native English tradition (Chaucer, Langland).
intellectual_concerns: Protestant nationalism and the reform of the church; virtue and courtesy as the disciplines of the self; Ireland and the ethics of colonization; mutability, time, and the poet's immortal fame; love and marriage as sacramental.
historical_significance: The greatest non-dramatic poet of the English Renaissance: The Faerie Queene created the English national epic and shaped the language's poetic tradition from Milton to Keats ('the poet's poet'), while Amoretti and Epithalamion founded the English marriage poem.
biographical_uncertainty: The year of birth rests on the sonnet 'Amoretti' 60's allusion and the records of his schooling; the exact circumstances of his final flight from Ireland and his poverty at death are reported by Ben Jonson and William Camden.

literary_identity: Courtier, soldier, diplomat, and poet; the model of the Renaissance man whose posthumously published works founded the English sonnet sequence and the critical defence of poetry.
biography: Born 30 November 1554 at Penshurst, eldest son of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at Shrewsbury School and Christ Church, Oxford, then travelled the continent (1572–75), witnessing the St Bartholomew's Day massacre and meeting continental humanists. At court he was a favourite of Elizabeth's diplomacy and a patron of letters (dedicatee of Spenser's Calender); his quarrel with the Earl of Oxford (1579) and his 'Letter to Queen Elizabeth' against the Anjou match (1579–80) marked his temporary rustication to Wilton, where he wrote the Arcadia. He served in Parliament, was knighted in 1583, and in 1585 was appointed governor of Flushing; he died on 17 October 1586 of a thigh wound received at Zutphen (famously giving his water to a dying soldier), and was mourned as the flower of English chivalry.
literary_profile: The courtier-poet who practised poetry as an aristocratic accomplishment rather than a profession — 'look in thy heart, and write'; his Defence of Poesy remains the period's central statement of the moral and cultural claims of literature, and Astrophel and Stella set the sonnet vogue of the 1590s in motion.
stylistic_characteristics: Elegant courtly wit, the first sustained English sonnet sequence with a narrative of courtship, the mingling of prose romance and eclogue in the Arcadia, and a critical prose of luminous argument.
intellectual_concerns: The defence of poetry against Puritan attack; the education of the aristocrat in virtue and action; the psychology of desire and self-knowledge; Protestant politics and the duties of the public man.
historical_significance: The posthumous publication of his works (Arcadia 1590, Astrophel and Stella 1591, The Defence of Poesy 1595) made him the tutelary genius of the 1590s literary generation and the English type of the poet-hero.
biographical_uncertainty: The dating of his major works rests on inference (the Arcadia is usually assigned to c. 1577–80, the Defence to c. 1579–81); none of his major works was printed in his lifetime by his own act.

full_name: Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke
literary_identity: Translator, poet, and literary patron; the sister of Sir Philip Sidney and the most important female literary figure of the Elizabethan period after the queen.
biography: Born 27 October 1561, daughter of Sir Henry Sidney; educated at home in French, Italian, and music. In 1577 she married Henry Herbert, second Earl of Pembroke, and made Wilton House a centre of letters; after her brother's death in 1586 she became his literary executrix, completing his verse translation of the Psalms (the Sidney Psalter) and supervising the publication of the Arcadia (1593). She translated Robert Garnier's Marc Antoine (1592) and Philippe de Mornay's Discours de la vie et de la mort (1592), wrote the pastoral dialogue for the queen's visit to Wilton (c. 1599), and patronized Spenser, Daniel, and Donne. She died of smallpox on 25 September 1621.
literary_profile: The presiding female patron of the Sidney circle, whose own translations — above all the 107 psalms of the Sidney Psalter — constitute one of the major poetic achievements of the period, uniting Reformed piety with the most sophisticated metrical experimentation in English.
stylistic_characteristics: Metrical virtuosity (the Psalter uses over 120 different verse forms), learned paraphrase, and a devotional voice of disciplined intensity.
intellectual_concerns: The Protestant poetics of the psalm tradition; the consolation of mortality; the continuation of her brother's literary and religious legacy; female authorship within the bounds of aristocratic propriety.
historical_significance: The first English woman to sustain a major literary career as patron, editor, translator, and poet; the Sidney Psalter influenced Donne and Herbert and stands as the great English monument of the Genevan psalm tradition.
biographical_uncertainty: The extent of her contribution to the Psalter (as against her brother's) is secure for Psalms 44–150; the degree of her editorial intervention in the 1593 Arcadia is debated.

literary_identity: Courtier, statesman, and poet; Sidney's closest friend and biographer, and the most philosophically austere of the Elizabethan sonneteers.
biography: Born 3 October 1554 into a Warwickshire gentry family; educated at Shrewsbury (with Sidney) and Jesus College, Cambridge. He served Elizabeth as treasurer of the navy and of war, and James I as chancellor of the Exchequer (1614–21), being created Baron Brooke in 1621. His poetry — Caelica, the treatises on monarchy and religion, and Mustapha and Alaham — circulated in manuscript in his lifetime; he was murdered on 30 September 1628 by a servant he had omitted from his will, and was buried in St Mary's, Warwick. His Life of the Renowned Sir Philip Sidney (printed 1652) is the classic memoir of the period.
literary_profile: A philosophical poet of power and dark inwardness whose verse dramas and treatises anatomize the corruptions of monarchy and the vanity of earthly desire; his Caelica turns the sonnet sequence into a meditation on the failure of worldly love and the turn to God.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, aphoristic, and abstract diction; Senecan sententiae; a Calvinist suspicion of the world expressed in sinewy couplets and dramatic choruses.
intellectual_concerns: The corruption of power and the duties of counsel; the vanity of human wishes; predestination and divine grace; the memory and meaning of Sidney's life and death.
historical_significance: The intellectual centre of the Sidney circle after Sidney's death; his poems and treatises form the most searching Elizabethan anatomy of politics and the soul outside Shakespeare and Donne.
biographical_uncertainty: His works were printed posthumously (1633, 1652) and the dating of Caelica's composition is approximate (c. 1580s–1610s).

literary_identity: Poet and historian; the author of Delia, one of the first of the 1590s sonnet sequences, and of the long poem The Civil Wars, tutor to Lady Anne Clifford.
biography: Born c. 1562 near Taunton, the son of a music master; educated at Magdalen Hall, Oxford. He served as tutor to William Herbert, later Earl of Pembroke, and travelled in Italy; his sonnet sequence Delia appeared in 1591–92 (appended to Astrophel and Stella in its first edition), followed by The Complaint of Rosamond (1592) and the tragedies Cleopatra (1594) and Philotas (1605). He was tutor to Lady Anne Clifford and groom of the chamber to Queen Anne; his Civil Wars (1595, revised to 1609) chronicled the Wars of the Roses. He died in October 1619 at Beckington, Somerset.
literary_profile: A laureate of moderate, musical verse — 'well-languaged Daniel' — whose sonnets, epistles, and philosophical poems (Musophilus, 1599) exemplify the Elizabethan ideal of learned eloquence in the service of moral reflection.
stylistic_characteristics: Smooth, balanced, sententious verse; the plain-style reaction against Petrarchan conceit; an Augustan moderation of diction and rhythm that anticipates the seventeenth century.
intellectual_concerns: The uses of history as moral example; the fortunes of kings and the instability of power; poetry as the civilizing art; constancy in love and in the self.
historical_significance: A principal shaper of the Elizabethan sonnet vogue and of the verse-epistle and historical poem; his influence ran to Milton and the Augustans, and his Delia's 'Care-charmer Sleep' remains a classic.
biographical_uncertainty: The year of birth (1562 or 1563) is uncertain; the extent of his rewriting of The Civil Wars across editions makes the poem's textual history complex.

literary_identity: Poet; the author of Idea, Poly-Olbion, and 'Since there's no help', the most prolific and professionally dedicated of the Elizabethan poets.
biography: Born 1563 at Hartshill, Warwickshire, where he served as a page in the household of Sir Henry Goodere; possibly at Oxford for a time. He settled in London in the 1590s as a professional writer, publishing the sonnet sequence Idea (1594, revised to 1619), the historical legends (Mortimeriados 1596, revised as The Barons' Wars 1603; England's Heroical Epistles 1597), the pastoral Endimion and Phoebe (1595), and the vast topographical poem Poly-Olbion (1612, 1622), before the late odes and elegies of his Poems (1619) and The Muses Elizium (1630). He died in London on 23 December 1631 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.
literary_profile: The period's most devoted professional poet, who ranged across every genre — sonnets, epistles, odes, pastorals, topography, satire, and the 'nymphidia' fairy verse — and revised his canon continuously across five decades.
stylistic_characteristics: Varied and capable rather than intense; the elegant sonnet, the sinewy epistle, the ambitious chorographical couplet of Poly-Olbion, and a late lyric grace ('Since there's no help, come let us kiss and part').
intellectual_concerns: English topography and the nation's antiquities; the historical memory of the Wars of the Roses; the poet's fame and the patronage system; love's vicissitudes.
historical_significance: The most complete professional man of letters of the age; Poly-Olbion is the great topographical poem of England, and his sonnets and odes remained in the anthologies that formed later English taste.
biographical_uncertainty: Details of his early life and of his alleged service to the Goodere family rest on late testimony; much of his early work survives only in his own revisions.

literary_identity: Playwright, poet, and actor; the central figure of English literature, author of some 39 plays, 154 sonnets, and two narrative poems.
biography: Baptized 26 April 1564 at Stratford-upon-Avon, son of the glover and alderman John Shakespeare; educated at the Stratford grammar school. He married Anne Hathaway in 1582 (children Susanna, and the twins Hamnet and Judith), and by 1592 was established in the London theatre (Greene's 'upstart crow' attack). He wrote for the Lord Chamberlain's Men (from 1594) and its successor the King's Men (from 1603), was a sharer in the Globe (1599) and Blackfriars, and prospered as actor, playwright, and investor, buying New Place in Stratford in 1597. The narrative poems Venus and Adonis (1593) and The Rape of Lucrece (1594) were his first printed works; the Sonnets appeared in 1609. He retired to Stratford around 1613 and died there on 23 April 1616; the First Folio of his plays was published by Heminges and Condell in 1623.
literary_profile: The supreme dramatist of the language and its greatest poet of the human interior: his histories, comedies, tragedies, and romances transformed every genre they touched, and his sonnets reinvented the Petrarchan sequence as a meditation on love, time, and art.
stylistic_characteristics: Unmatched range of register — from the euphuistic wit and sonneteering of the early plays to the metaphysical density of the great tragedies and the late romances' verse of reconciliation; mastery of blank verse, prose, and song; the invention of character through soliloquy.
intellectual_concerns: Kingship, legitimacy, and the body politic; love, jealousy, and self-deception; time, mortality, and the immortality of art; the theatre itself as the mirror of nature; conscience and the divided self.
historical_significance: The measure of English literature: his works constitute the largest single achievement of the language's canon, translated into every tongue and performed continuously since the 1590s.
biographical_uncertainty: The chronology of the plays rests on printed dates, records of performance, and stylistic evidence; the authorship of several plays (Titus Andronicus, Pericles, Henry VIII, The Two Noble Kinsmen, Edward III, Sir Thomas More) is collaborative, and the biographical record between 1585 and 1592 is a blank.

literary_identity: Playwright, poet, and translator; the creator of the Elizabethan tragic stage and of the 'mighty line' of blank verse.
biography: Baptized 26 February 1564 at Canterbury, son of a shoemaker; a King's Scholar at the King's School, Canterbury, and a Parker Scholar at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge (BA 1584, MA 1587, the latter after the Privy Council intervened over his absences, plausibly for government service). In London he wrote Tamburlaine (1587–88), Doctor Faustus (c. 1588–92), The Jew of Malta (c. 1589–90), Edward II (c. 1592), and The Massacre at Paris (c. 1592–93), and translated Ovid's Amores and Lucan's Pharsalia I. He was associated with Ralegh's circle and suspected of atheism (the 'Baines note'); on 30 May 1593 he was killed in a quarrel at a Deptford house by Ingram Frizer, the coroner recording the stabbing as self-defence in a dispute over the reckoning.
literary_profile: The founder of Elizabethan tragedy: Tamburlaine's conquering rhetoric, Faustus's aspiring intellect, Barabas's satanic wit, and Edward II's study of a king's fall created the overreacher and the tragic stage that Shakespeare inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: The 'mighty line' — muscular, end-stopped blank verse of enormous rhetorical force; the set-piece oration; lyric interludes ('Come live with me'); ironic juxtaposition of grandeur and brutality.
intellectual_concerns: The limits of human aspiration — power, knowledge, wealth, desire; Machiavellian statecraft; religious scepticism and the fear of damnation; the collision of the individual will with the order of things.
historical_significance: The greatest dramatic innovator before Shakespeare: he made blank verse the language of the stage, created the Elizabethan history play and tragedy, and his life and death — poet, spy, atheist — became the legend of the Elizabethan imagination.
biographical_uncertainty: The dates of the plays rest on publication and performance records (none of the plays was printed in his lifetime); the circumstances of his death, his alleged espionage, and the authorship of parts of his canon (Dido with Nashe, the Henry VI plays) remain debated.

literary_identity: Playwright, poet, and critic; the first great English literary professional and the presiding classicist of the Jacobean stage, author of the comedies of humours, the masques, and 'To Penshurst'.
biography: Born June 1572 in Westminster (posthumous son of a clergyman), educated at Westminster School under William Camden, and briefly a bricklayer (his stepfather's trade) before soldiering in Flanders. By 1597 he was acting and writing for Henslowe (imprisoned in 1598 for killing the actor Gabriel Spencer in a duel, escaping hanging by benefit of clergy); Every Man in His Humour (1598, with Shakespeare in the cast) made his name. The comedies Volpone (1606), Epicene (1609), The Alchemist (1610), and Bartholomew Fair (1614) and the tragedies Sejanus (1603) and Catiline (1611) followed, together with the masques written with Inigo Jones for the Jacobean court (1605–31). He published his Works in folio in 1616 — the first English playwright to do so — and died on 6 August 1637, buried upright in Westminster Abbey ('O rare Ben Jonson').
literary_profile: The laureate of the Stuart court and the legislator of classical taste: his comedies anatomize human folly through the theory of humours, his poems ('Drink to me only', the Cary–Morison ode, the epitaphs) set the standard of English neoclassical lyric, and his Timber is the period's major critical commonplace book.
stylistic_characteristics: Classical discipline and satirical vigour; the humours theory of character; erudite, plain-style verse of great metrical skill; the masque's fusion of poetry, spectacle, and antimasque.
intellectual_concerns: The moral function of poetry and satire; the correction of folly and vice; classical imitation and the English claim to Augustan standing; patronage, fame, and the writer's craft.
historical_significance: The first English author to treat writing as a profession and the canon as a curated Works; his comedies and critical authority shaped English drama and letters for a century, and his 'tribe of Ben' founded the Cavalier lyric.
biographical_uncertainty: The year of birth (1572 or 1573) is inferred; the canon of his collaborations (with Chapman, Marston, and others) and the lost plays are matters of scholarly reconstruction.

literary_identity: Poet, preacher, and Dean of St Paul's; the greatest of the metaphysical poets, author of the Songs and Sonnets, the Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries, the Devotions, and the sermons.
biography: Born in London in 1572 into a recusant Catholic family (his mother was a daughter of John Heywood, and his uncle Jasper Heywood led the Jesuits); educated at Hart Hall, Oxford, and possibly Cambridge, and at Lincoln's Inn. He sailed on the Cadiz (1596) and Islands (1597) expeditions and was secretary to Sir Thomas Egerton before his secret marriage to Egerton's niece Anne More in 1601 wrecked his secular career ('John Donne, Anne Donne, Un-done'). After years of poverty and patronage-seeking, he took orders in 1615 at the king's urging, became Reader at Lincoln's Inn, Dean of St Paul's (1621), and the most famous preacher of the age. His poems circulated in manuscript in his lifetime (the Songs and Sonnets, Elegies, Satires, Holy Sonnets, the Anniversaries of 1611–12 on Elizabeth Drury); the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions appeared in 1624; the poems were first collected in 1633. He died on 31 March 1631 after preaching his own funeral sermon, 'Death's Duel'.
literary_profile: The poet of wit and the preacher of love: the Songs and Sonnets and Elegies are the great secular lyrics of the period, the Holy Sonnets and 'Good Friday, 1613. Riding Westward' its great devotional poems, and the sermons the summit of English pulpit prose.
stylistic_characteristics: The dramatic opening, the extended conceit, the colloquial vehemence of an argumentative line, paradox and hyperbole, and the union of the erotic and the divine; in the sermons, a baroque prose of enormous periodic energy.
intellectual_concerns: The inseparability of body and soul; constancy and inconstancy in love; death, judgement, and resurrection; the discovery of the new philosophy and the decay of the old cosmos; the self as microcosm.
historical_significance: The greatest English metaphysical poet and one of the supreme preachers: his poetry was rediscovered by Grierson (1912) and Eliot as the alternative tradition to Spenserian sweetness, and shaped twentieth-century poetry; his Devotions ('No man is an island') and sermons remain classics of prose.
biographical_uncertainty: Nearly all the poems are undated and circulated in widely varying manuscripts; the canon and ordering of the Songs and Sonnets depend on the 1633 and 1635 editions; several elegies' attributions remain contested.

literary_identity: Poet, composer, and physician; the supreme English writer of the lute song, author of the airs and of the treatise on English metre Observations in the Art of English Poesy.
biography: Born 12 February 1567 in London; educated at Peterhouse, Cambridge, and Gray's Inn, and took his medical degree at the University of Caen (1605), practising medicine in London. He published the Latin Poemata (1595), Observations in the Art of English Poesy (1602), the masque for Lord Hayes (1607), and above all the songbooks A Book of Airs (1601, with Philip Rosseter) and the Two, Third, and Fourth Books of Airs (c. 1613–17), for which he wrote both words and music. He died in London on 1 March 1620.
literary_profile: The one English poet-composer of the first rank: his airs — 'When to her lute Corinna sings', 'Rose-cheeked Laura', 'Never weather-beaten sail' — wed the Elizabethan lyric to the continental lute song with a musical economy unmatched in the language.
stylistic_characteristics: Quantitative experiments in Latin and English; short-lined, song-like verse of classical restraint; an anti-rhyming polemic in the Observations belied by his own masterly rhymes.
intellectual_concerns: The union of music and poetry; classical prosody and the reform of English metre; the pleasures and deceits of love; moral and religious consolation.
historical_significance: The summit of the English lute-song tradition and a major figure in the history of English prosody; his airs remained in performance and shaped the lyric taste of the seventeenth century.
biographical_uncertainty: The attribution of several poems between Campion and his collaborators (notably Rosseter) is partly editorial; the dates of the later songbooks are inferred.

literary_identity: Lawyer, statesman, and poet; author of Orchestra and Nosce Teipsum, the most accomplished philosophical poems of the Elizabethan period, and later attorney-general for Ireland.
biography: Born in 1569 in Wiltshire; educated at Winchester and the Queen's College, Oxford, and the Middle Temple (called to the bar 1595). His Orchestra, or A Poem of Dancing was published in 1596, and Nosce Teipsum in 1599, both dedicated to Queen Elizabeth; he was disbarred in 1598 for striking Richard Martin in the Middle Temple hall, restored in 1601, and sat in the parliaments of James I. As solicitor-general (1603) and attorney-general (1606) for Ireland he administered the Ulster plantation and became speaker of the Irish parliament (1613); he returned to England as a judge in 1619, was lord chief justice briefly in 1626, and died on 8 December 1626.
literary_profile: A philosophical poet of unusual lucidity who turned the hardest questions of the soul into polished quatrains; Nosce Teipsum ('Know thyself') was celebrated by contemporaries as the proof that English verse could reason.
stylistic_characteristics: The decasyllabic quatrain used with argumentative precision; elegant metaphysical wit without obscurity; the marriage of law, philosophy, and verse.
intellectual_concerns: The immortality of the soul and the nature of knowledge; the cosmic order expressed in the dance (Orchestra); the union of poetry and philosophy; the reform of Ireland and the duties of the magistrate.
historical_significance: The finest English philosophical poet before the metaphysicals, whose Nosce Teipsum was admired by Coleridge and remains the classic Elizabethan poem of self-knowledge.
biographical_uncertainty: The poems' dates are approximate; the attribution of several epigrams between Sir John Davies and John Davies of Hereford has been a source of confusion since the seventeenth century.
